new_statements.quote: p.73: "Under suprasegmental phonetics and phonology, I discuss tone and intonation in Hyow. Though tone, stress and intonation are traditionally known as suprasegmental features, they are necessarily realization of pitch modification of segments that allow the process. Hyow utilize only tone and intonation as suprasegmental features. Compared to tone, intonation is less vital in the phonetics and phonology of Hyow." p.22: "Hyow is a tonal language with three lexical tones – high level (H), low level (L) and high falling (F). ... The Laitu dialect in Myanmar has one convex tone and two falling tones, which are recognized as high, mid and low in the orthography."

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is described as lexically (and grammatically) tonal with three tones; stress is explicitly excluded from its suprasegmental system -- only tone and intonation are used. Unlike neighbouring Southern Chin languages (Sumtu, Daai, Lemi), polysyllables do not carry reduced/sesquisyllabic initial syllables (prefix vowels harmonize with the root vowel instead), so no iambic minor-major stress profile is posited. For the Myanmar (clj) Laitu variety specifically the source gives only the tone inventory (one convex, two falling tones).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Only two sesquisyllabic words exist in (Bangladesh) Hyow (p.72). Tone systems differ across varieties: Kontu two falling tones; western Gungrupara Laitu two rising tones; Myanmar Laitu one convex + two falling.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level suprasegmentals; the tonal analysis and the 'only tone and intonation' statement rest on Eastern Gungrupara Laitu Hyow (Bandarban, Bangladesh) recorded in isolation and carrier sentences; Myanmar Laitu data come from a wordlist recorded in Yangon plus later ELDP fieldwork in Minbya. Intonation treated separately (sec. 2.6.2, phrase level).
new_statements.identity_note: lait1239 is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING code ('Pending Report Release') for ISO clj = Laitu of Minbya/Mrauk-U/Myebon, Rakhine State. The quoted source (Zakaria 2018) is principally a grammar of Laitu HYOW of Gungrupara, Bandarban, Bangladesh (Khyang; Glottolog files this grammar under asho1236 Asho Chin > khya1239 Khyang, and the asho1236 audit folder already holds the same file). Zakaria explicitly treats the Myanmar Laitu of Mrauk-U/Minbya/Myebon (i.e. clj) as a dialect of the same language ('The Laitu dialect in Myanmar...', p.22; fieldwork with Minbya/Mrauk-U Laitu and a later ELDP project in Minbya), but notes its tone system differs (one convex + two falling tones vs H/L/F). So the 'tone and intonation only, no stress' statement is first-hand for Bangladesh Laitu Hyow and only by the author's extension for clj; the catalog must not count Zakaria 2018 as two independent descriptions (asho1236/khya1239 and lait1239). Lew 2019 indicates three Laitu varieties in Myanmar covered by the 2013 orthography.

sources.locator: Ch. 2 sec. 2.6 'Suprasegmental phonetics and phonology', p. 73 (PDF p. 104); supporting: sec. 1.9.1 p. 22 (PDF p. 53) on the Myanmar Laitu tone inventory; sec. 2.5 p. 72 on absence of reduced (sesqui)syllables.
sources.note: Sec. 2.6 p.73: 'Hyow utilize only tone and intonation as suprasegmental features' -- stress explicitly not among them; three lexical tones H, L, F (analysis based on Eastern Gungrupara Laitu Hyow, Bangladesh). Sec. 1.9.1 p.22: 'The Laitu dialect in Myanmar has one convex tone and two falling tones, which are recognized as high, mid and low in the orthography' (this is the clj variety of Minbya). p.72: Hyow polysyllables lack the reduced/sesquisyllabic initial syllables of Sumtu, Daai, Lemi. The author did fieldwork with Laitu of Mrauk-U/Minbya and treats Myanmar Laitu as a dialect of Hyow.

sources.citation: Lew, Sigrid. 2019. Proposing a Facilitated Participatory Approach for Southeast Asian Minority Language Orthography Design. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 12.1: lxvii-lxxv. hdl:10524/52451.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone values. Reports (p. lxxi-lxxii) that the author 'was asked to perform a phonological analysis and revise the existing orthography' of Laitu Chin (workshop 2007; orthography revised 2013 'to comprise three Laitu varieties'). That phonological analysis is unpublished.
